title: Major Anatomical Divisions and Subdivisions of the Brain
summary: A guided tour of the brain: how it is protected, the forebrain and cerebrum, the thalamus, hypothalamus and limbic system, and the midbrain, hindbrain and cerebellum.

lesson.title: The body's control centre
lesson.hook: An okada rider who falls without a helmet may walk away with a scratch, or lose the ability to speak. Same fall, different damage. Why? Because each part of the brain does a different job.

slides.heading: A complex control centre
slides.body:
The human brain is the **control centre** of the body. It contains **billions of neural connections** working together, and different parts handle **specific functions**. Injury to one part can rob a person of particular abilities, which is why knowing brain anatomy helps us understand **traumatic brain injury**.

The adult brain weighs roughly **1.3 to 1.4 kg** and looks whitish-pink.

slides.heading: Brain, nerves and spinal cord
slides.body:
The brain sends messages along **nerves**, like cables carried on poles across a city. Some nerves link directly to the brain; others reach it through the **spinal cord** running down the back.

The **brain and spinal cord** together form the **central nervous system (CNS)**. The brain controls organs and also **thinks and remembers**, the activity we often call the mind.

steps.title: The cranium
steps.detail: Eight interlocking skull bones give maximum protection for minimum weight.

steps.title: Cerebrospinal fluid
steps.detail: Made by the choroid plexuses, this fluid lets the brain float and cushions it.

steps.title: Blood-brain barrier
steps.detail: Special capillaries filter out harmful chemicals but let oxygen, water and glucose in.

slides.heading: A hungry organ
slides.body:
The brain is only about 2% of body weight, yet it receives **nearly one-fifth of the blood** the heart pumps. A dense network of vessels carries that blood, with its oxygen and glucose, to where it is needed.

This is why a **stroke**, which cuts blood supply to part of the brain, can cause damage within minutes.

slides.question: Which structure filters harmful chemicals out of the blood but lets oxygen and glucose reach the brain?
slides.why: The blood-brain barrier is a network of specialised capillaries acting as a filter. The choroid plexuses produce cerebrospinal fluid.

terms.meaning: Cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus and limbic structures
Tectum and tegmentum, with the substantia nigra
Medulla, pons and midbrain (often with the diencephalon), linking brain and spinal cord

slides.heading: The cerebrum
slides.body:
The **cerebrum** is the **largest part** of the brain and handles **higher functions** such as thought, language and planned action. Its thin, folded outer layer is the **cerebral cortex**; beneath it lie **subcortical** structures: thalamus, hypothalamus, limbic system and basal ganglia.

The brain's **anatomy** is largely **hierarchical**, but its **working** organisation is not: parts at many levels cooperate (Bloom et al., 2001).

slides.heading: Two injuries, two outcomes
slides.story: Two okada riders fall on the same Ibadan road. Emeka hits the back of his head and the brainstem is shaken: his breathing needs support in the emergency room. Sola hits the front: he breathes normally but later struggles to plan his day and control his temper. Same accident, different parts of the brain hurt.
slides.takeaway: Because each brain region has its own job, where an injury lands decides which abilities are lost.

slides.heading: Two hemispheres, one bridge
slides.body:
A deep groove divides the forebrain into **left and right hemispheres**. They look nearly symmetrical but work slightly differently. Popular accounts link the **left** with **language and logic** and the **right** with **spatial and creative** tasks, though real abilities draw on both sides.

The **corpus callosum**, a thick bundle of axons, connects the two hemispheres so they can share information.

slides.question: The bundle of axons that connects the left and right hemispheres is the:
slides.why: The corpus callosum is the main bridge between the hemispheres. The pons is a bridge in the brainstem.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'identify the parts of the brain' and 'discuss the anatomical organisation of the brain'. Learn which structures belong to forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain, and the three protections. Objectives test the blood-brain barrier versus choroid plexus, and cortex versus subcortex. Trap: putting the thalamus in the midbrain; it is forebrain.
slides.sampleQuestion: Which of the following is NOT a forebrain structure? (a) cerebrum (b) thalamus (c) hypothalamus (d) medulla
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (d): the medulla is in the hindbrain. Present the three divisions as a table in essays.

points: Brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system.
Protection: cranium, cerebrospinal fluid, blood-brain barrier.
Three divisions: forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain.
The cerebrum is largest; its outer layer is the cortex.
Two hemispheres are linked by the corpus callosum.

questions.stem: The central nervous system is made up of:
options: Brain and nerves in the limbs
questions.explanation: The CNS is the brain plus the spinal cord; other nerves form the peripheral system.

questions.stem: The largest part of the human brain is the:
questions.explanation: The cerebrum is the largest part and handles higher functions.

questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced by the:
questions.explanation: Specialised vessels called choroid plexuses make cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.stem: The cranium is formed by how many interlocking skull bones?
questions.explanation: Eight interlocking plates form the cranium.

questions.stem: Which of these is a subcortical structure?
questions.explanation: The thalamus lies beneath the cortex, so it is subcortical.

questions.stem: The blood-brain barrier allows which of the following into the brain?
questions.explanation: It filters out many harmful substances but admits essentials like oxygen, water and glucose.

questions.stem: A patient whose corpus callosum has been cut would most likely have difficulty with:
options: Sharing information between the two hemispheres
questions.explanation: The corpus callosum connects the hemispheres; cutting it limits communication between them.

questions.stem: A stroke causes rapid damage mainly because the brain:
options: Depends on a constant blood supply carrying oxygen and glucose
questions.explanation: The brain uses about a fifth of the heart's output and has little reserve, so loss of blood flow quickly harms it.

questions.stem: A head blow that leaves a person unable to plan or reason but able to breathe normally most likely damaged the:
questions.explanation: Planning and reasoning are higher functions of the cerebrum; breathing is controlled by the brainstem.

questions.stem: All of the following protect the brain EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The corpus callosum connects hemispheres; it is not a protective structure.

questions.stem: Bloom and colleagues (2001) noted that the brain's organisation is:
options: Hierarchical in anatomy but not in operation
Hierarchical in both anatomy and operation
questions.explanation: Its structure is layered, but its parts work together across levels rather than in a strict chain of command.

questions.stem: Which pairing of division and structure is correct?
questions.explanation: The pons is in the hindbrain. The cerebellum and medulla are hindbrain; the hypothalamus is forebrain.

questions.stem: I. The brain receives nearly a fifth of the heart's blood output. II. The blood-brain barrier blocks glucose. III. Cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. II is wrong: glucose passes the barrier because the brain needs it.

questions.stem: Why is the popular claim that the 'left brain is logical and the right brain is creative' treated with caution?
options: Hemispheres differ somewhat, but complex abilities draw on both sides working together
The corpus callosum prevents any difference
questions.explanation: There are real differences, but most abilities involve both hemispheres communicating through the corpus callosum.

questions.stem: A drug designed to act on brain cells fails because it cannot reach them from the bloodstream. The most likely reason is the:
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier filters many substances, which is a major challenge in designing brain drugs.

lesson.title: Relay, regulator and emotion
lesson.hook: You are reading this sentence while ignoring the fan, the traffic and your own heartbeat. A small structure deep in your brain is deciding which signals reach your awareness right now.

slides.heading: The thalamus: a hub
slides.body:
The **thalamus** is often called a **switching centre**. Kosslyn and Rosenberg (2006) compare it to an **airline hub** where planes converge and then fly off to distant places.

Signals from the **senses**, such as vision and hearing, and from **motor** systems pass through the thalamus, which **routes** them to the right parts of the cortex. (Smell is the main exception.)

slides.heading: Attention, sleep and survival
slides.body:
The thalamus also helps with **attention**: it is helping you focus on each word right now. It plays a part in **sleep** control too.

Its role is so critical that **severe thalamic damage can be fatal**, even if the cortex is untouched.

slides.heading: The hypothalamus: small but vital
slides.body:
The **hypothalamus** sits **under** the thalamus and makes up only about **3%** of the brain (Hofman & Swaab, 1992). Yet it controls **eating and drinking**, **body temperature**, **blood pressure**, **heart rate** and **sexual behaviour** (Swaab, 2003).

It also triggers hormones that prepare the body to **fight or flee** when facing danger.

left.title: Neural messages
points: Regulate the autonomic nervous system
Sympathetic and parasympathetic
Reach other brain areas

right.title: Chemical messages
points: Regulate endocrine glands
Signal the pituitary
Control hormone release

slides.question: Which structure regulates hunger, thirst and body temperature?
slides.why: The hypothalamus keeps the body in balance (homeostasis). The thalamus mainly relays sensory signals.

slides.heading: When the hypothalamus fails
slides.body:
Damage or disorder of the hypothalamus can cause a range of problems: **memory loss**, **depression**, **low body temperature**, **overeating**, **diabetes-like** symptoms and **chronic drowsiness** (Martin & Riskind, 1992).

The variety of symptoms reflects how many body systems it keeps in balance.

slides.heading: The limbic system
slides.body:
The **limbic system** lies close to the hypothalamus, between the thalamus and the cortex. It includes the **amygdala** and **hippocampus**, and is involved in **emotion, motivation**, food and water intake and **homeostasis**.

The **amygdala**, named from the Greek for **almond**, is central to **fear and anger** and even to reading emotion in faces (Adolphs et al., 1996).

slides.heading: The basal ganglia
slides.body:
The **basal ganglia** lie on the outer sides of the thalami. They help **plan and produce movement** and play a key role in forming **habits**.

They depend heavily on the neurotransmitter **dopamine**. In **Parkinson's disease**, loss of dopamine input to the basal ganglia leads to tremor, stiffness and difficulty starting movements.

slides.heading: The dog at the gate
slides.story: Adaeze walks past a gate and a large dog suddenly barks. Before she even thinks, her heart races, her breathing speeds up and she jumps back. Her amygdala detected danger; her hypothalamus fired the fight-or-flight response through the autonomic nervous system and hormones.
slides.takeaway: The amygdala and hypothalamus work together to produce fast emotional and bodily reactions to threat.

slides.question: Parkinson's disease is linked to problems with which structure and neurotransmitter?
slides.why: The basal ganglia depend on dopamine; its loss causes Parkinson's movement problems.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Common: 'describe the thalamus' and 'do the thalamus and hypothalamus perform the same function?'. Answer: no; one relays, the other regulates. Objectives test the airline-hub analogy, the 3% figure, the almond-shaped amygdala, and Parkinson's with dopamine. Know the two kinds of hypothalamic messages.
slides.sampleQuestion: Distinguish between the thalamus and the hypothalamus in location and function.
slides.howToAnswer: Thalamus: above, relays sensory and motor signals to the cortex, aids attention and sleep. Hypothalamus: below it, about 3% of the brain, regulates homeostasis through autonomic nerves and hormones.

points: Thalamus: relay hub for sensory and motor signals; attention and sleep.
Hypothalamus: ~3% of brain; hunger, thirst, temperature, hormones.
It sends neural (autonomic) and chemical (endocrine) messages.
Limbic system: emotion and motivation; amygdala for fear and anger.
Basal ganglia: movement and habits; dopamine; Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: The thalamus is often compared to a:
questions.explanation: It routes incoming signals to the right brain areas, like a hub.

questions.stem: The amygdala's name comes from the Greek word for:
questions.explanation: Amygdala means almond, after its shape. Hippocampus means seahorse.

questions.stem: The hypothalamus makes up roughly what proportion of the brain?
questions.explanation: It is tiny, about 3%, yet controls many vital functions.

questions.stem: The hypothalamus regulates the endocrine system mainly through:
questions.explanation: Its chemical messages control endocrine glands, notably via the pituitary.

questions.stem: The basal ganglia are mainly involved in:
options: Planning and producing movement and forming habits
questions.explanation: They support movement and habit learning, relying on dopamine.

questions.stem: Severe damage to the thalamus can be fatal because:
options: It plays critical roles in routing signals, attention and sleep
questions.explanation: Its relay and arousal roles are so vital that serious damage can kill even if the cortex survives.

questions.stem: A patient after a tumour near the base of the brain eats constantly, feels cold and is always drowsy. The structure most likely affected is the:
questions.explanation: Overeating, low temperature and drowsiness are signs of hypothalamic disorder.

questions.stem: A woman with amygdala damage cannot tell when faces look frightened. This supports the amygdala's role in:
questions.explanation: The amygdala is linked to fear and to reading emotional expressions.

questions.stem: An elderly man shows hand tremor and struggles to start walking. Doctors suspect loss of dopamine affecting the:
questions.explanation: These are classic Parkinson's signs, linked to dopamine and the basal ganglia.

questions.stem: All of the following are functions of the hypothalamus EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Connecting hemispheres is the corpus callosum's job.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: The amygdala handles fear and anger. The thalamus relays; the hypothalamus regulates homeostasis.

questions.stem: The hypothalamus's neural messages mainly regulate the:
questions.explanation: Neural messages regulate sympathetic and parasympathetic activity; chemical messages regulate glands.

questions.stem: I. The thalamus relays most sensory signals to the cortex. II. The hypothalamus sits above the thalamus. III. The limbic system includes the amygdala and hippocampus. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. II is reversed: the hypothalamus lies under the thalamus.

questions.stem: Do the thalamus and hypothalamus perform the same function?
options: No: the thalamus controls emotion only
No: the thalamus relays signals, the hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and hormones
questions.explanation: They are neighbours with different jobs: relay versus regulation.

questions.stem: A researcher finds that rats with basal ganglia damage can learn new facts but struggle to form automatic habits. This supports the role of the basal ganglia in:
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia are critical for habit learning, distinct from fact-based memory.

lesson.title: Life support and coordination
lesson.hook: A police officer asks a suspected drunk driver to walk a straight line and touch his nose. That test is really checking one part of the brain. Which one?

slides.heading: The midbrain
slides.body:
The **midbrain** lies between the forebrain and hindbrain, above the pons. It surrounds the **cerebral aqueduct**, the channel linking the third and fourth ventricles.

Its main parts are the **tectum** (roof) and **tegmentum**, along with the **substantia nigra**. The tegmentum carries fibre tracts between hindbrain and forebrain and has nuclei controlling **eye muscles**.

left.title: Superior colliculi
points: Upper pair of bumps
Input from the optic nerves
Visual reflexes

right.title: Inferior colliculi
points: Lower pair of bumps
Hearing and auditory reflexes
Locate sounds by timing at each ear

slides.heading: Substantia nigra
slides.body:
The **substantia nigra**, meaning '**black substance**' for its dark pigment, is closely linked to the **basal ganglia**. Its neurons supply **dopamine** that helps process motor commands from higher centres.

Its **degeneration** is the hallmark of **Parkinson's disease**, which makes movement difficult.

slides.heading: Reticular activating system
slides.body:
The **reticular activating system (RAS)** is a diffuse network running from the **medulla and pons** through the **midbrain** towards the forebrain.

Its fibres rising to the **cortex** produce a general state of **arousal and wakefulness** (Steriade, 1996). The related **reticular formation** (Latin *reticulum*, 'network') regulates **sleep and arousal**.

slides.question: The inferior colliculi are mainly involved in:
slides.why: The inferior colliculi handle auditory processing and reflexes. The superior colliculi handle visual input.

slides.heading: The medulla: life support
slides.body:
The **medulla** (medulla oblongata) is the lowest part of the brain, just above the spinal cord. Nearly all information passing between the brain and body travels through it.

Its **nuclei** control **breathing, heart rate and blood pressure**, and some give rise to **cranial nerves**. Because these functions are vital, **damage to the medulla is quickly fatal**.

slides.heading: The pons: a bridge
slides.body:
**Pons** is Latin for **bridge**. It connects the **medulla** with higher centres and with the **cerebellum**.

It contains the **cochlear nucleus** (sound) and **vestibular nucleus** (balance). Nuclei in the pons are needed for **REM sleep**, and the **raphe nuclei** and **locus coeruleus** project widely to influence arousal and sleep.

slides.heading: The cerebellum: little brain
slides.body:
The **cerebellum** ('little brain' in Latin) sits at the back of the brainstem. Cut lengthwise, its white matter forms a **tree-like** pattern.

It **coordinates voluntary movement**, maintains **muscle tone** and regulates **balance**. It combines input about where the body **is** (from the spinal cord) with what you **intend** to do (from the cortex via the pons) and works out the sequence of muscle actions. It also stores learned motor routines.

slides.heading: The roadside sobriety test
slides.story: At a checkpoint, an officer asks a driver to walk heel to toe and touch his nose with eyes closed. The driver sways and misses. Alcohol affects the cerebellum early, so these simple tests of coordination are really tests of cerebellar function. Slurred, uneven speech is another sign.
slides.takeaway: Cerebellar damage or intoxication disrupts skilled, coordinated movement, balance and speech.

slides.question: Damage to which structure is most rapidly fatal because it controls breathing and heart rate?
slides.why: The medulla's nuclei control vital functions, so damage there quickly kills.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'describe the midbrain and the hindbrain'. Name the parts and functions. Objectives love: superior versus inferior colliculi, substantia nigra ('black substance') and Parkinson's, pons ('bridge') and REM sleep, cerebellum and sobriety tests. Trap: confusing the medulla (vital functions) with the cerebellum (coordination).
slides.sampleQuestion: Which hindbrain structure contains nuclei necessary for REM sleep? (a) medulla (b) pons (c) cerebellum (d) tectum
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). Then list the three hindbrain parts with one function each: medulla (vital functions), pons (bridge, REM sleep), cerebellum (coordination).

points: Midbrain: tectum (colliculi) and tegmentum; substantia nigra.
Superior colliculi: vision; inferior colliculi: hearing.
RAS and reticular formation: arousal and sleep.
Medulla: breathing, heart rate, blood pressure; damage fatal.
Pons: bridge, REM sleep; cerebellum: coordination, balance, alcohol-sensitive.

questions.stem: The three main parts of the hindbrain are:
questions.explanation: The hindbrain consists of the medulla, pons and cerebellum.

questions.stem: 'Pons' means:
questions.explanation: Pons is Latin for bridge; cerebellum means little brain.

questions.stem: The cerebellum is mainly responsible for:
questions.explanation: It coordinates movement, maintains muscle tone and regulates balance.

questions.stem: The superior colliculi receive input from the:
questions.explanation: The superior colliculi handle visual input; the inferior colliculi handle hearing.

questions.stem: Degeneration of the substantia nigra is associated with:
questions.explanation: Loss of dopamine neurons there underlies Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: The reticular activating system is responsible for:
questions.explanation: Its fibres activate the cortex to produce arousal.

questions.stem: A man turns his head instantly towards a sudden car horn on his left. This auditory reflex involves the:
questions.explanation: The inferior colliculi support auditory reflexes and sound localisation.

questions.stem: A patient after a brainstem stroke cannot enter REM sleep. Damage most likely involves the:
questions.explanation: Nuclei in the pons are necessary for REM sleep.

questions.stem: A footballer after a head injury walks unsteadily and slurs some words. The most likely damaged structure is the:
questions.explanation: Unsteady gait and slurred speech are classic cerebellar signs.

questions.stem: All of the following are found in or associated with the midbrain EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The medulla is part of the hindbrain.

questions.stem: Why are roadside sobriety tests effectively tests of cerebellar function?
options: Alcohol affects the cerebellum early, disrupting coordination and balance
questions.explanation: The cerebellum is among the first structures affected by alcohol, so coordination tests reveal intoxication.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: The pons contains the cochlear (sound) and vestibular (balance) nuclei.

questions.stem: I. The medulla controls breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. II. The cerebellum receives information about intended movements from the cortex via the pons. III. The inferior colliculi receive input from the optic nerves. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. III is wrong: the superior colliculi receive optic input.

questions.stem: The cerebellum works out the sequence of muscle movements by combining:
options: Current body position from the spinal cord and intended movement from the cortex
questions.explanation: It compares where the body is with what the cortex plans, then coordinates the movement.

questions.stem: A patient is in a prolonged coma though the cortex appears intact. Damage to which system could best explain the loss of arousal?
questions.explanation: The RAS activates the cortex; without it, the cortex cannot maintain wakefulness.
